teaser: A government scandal painted the size of a wall, with a rescue ship you can barely see.

lesson.text: This canvas was built for one room: the big square gallery of the Louvre where, every year or two, the French state held its official exhibition, the Salon. Walls were covered from floor to ceiling. To be noticed there, a young painter needed size. Théodore Géricault, 27, brought a picture about 5 meters high and 7 wide (roughly 16 by 23 feet).

Canvases that large were reserved for kings, saints and ancient heroes. Géricault filled his with something from the newspapers: a shipwreck only three years old, which the government badly wanted forgotten. In the Salon booklet it was listed under a careful, vague title, “Shipwreck Scene.” Everybody knew which shipwreck.

In July 1816 the navy frigate Medusa ran aground off the coast of West Africa. Its captain owed his post to royal favor and had hardly sailed in twenty years. He and the senior passengers took the lifeboats. About 147 other people were crowded onto a raft knocked together from masts and planks, roughly 20 by 7 meters (65 by 23 feet).

The boats were supposed to tow the raft. The ropes were let go. Thirteen days later, fifteen people were still alive on it. In between came storms, mutiny, thirst, madness and cannibalism. Géricault had all of that to choose from. He chose the morning a sail appeared on the horizon.
The rescue ship, the Argus, is in the painting. It is far smaller than you expect. Can you spot it?

spots.title: The Argus
spots.text: A pale speck on the horizon, to the right of the waving figures. Géricault made it tiny on purpose: that day the ship sailed on without seeing them. It came back only hours later.

lesson.text: So the picture does not show a rescue. It shows the instant of not knowing. Everything in it is organized around that speck, and around the distance between it and the men. To hold twenty bodies together, Géricault needed a strong skeleton under the chaos.
Three lines carry the whole composition, the way the parts of a picture are arranged.

lines.label: The climb
lines.text: From the dead at the lower left to the man waving at the top, bodies rise like a wave. Read along it and you pass from despair to exhaustion to hope.

lines.label: The mast
lines.text: Mast and ropes form a second, darker pyramid on the left. Its point leans away from the rescue ship.

lines.label: The wind
lines.text: The sail swells toward the left. The wind is pushing the raft away from the Argus, straight toward the dark wave rising at the left edge.

lesson.text: Two forces pull against each other: human arms straining to the right, wind and sea dragging to the left. The painting holds its breath between them.

Géricault tracked down two survivors, the surgeon Savigny and the engineer Corréard, whose published account had caused the scandal. He also found the raft's carpenter and had him build a scale model of it for the studio.

He rented a studio large enough for the canvas, close to a hospital, and worked there for months almost without going out. He studied the sick and the dying, and brought back severed limbs from the morgue to learn the color of dead flesh. Friends remembered the smell. He is said to have shaved his head so he would not be tempted to go to parties.

And yet the people on his raft are not the skeletal, sunburned, bearded survivors of the reports. They have the heavy shoulders of ancient statues and of Michelangelo's figures. Critics noticed. Géricault wanted the dignity of grand painting for ordinary, anonymous victims.

lesson.title: Four people
lesson.text: Follow the climb from bottom left to top right and meet four of the figures.

spots.title: The father
spots.text: An older man holds a dead youth across his knees and stares at nothing. He is the only one who has turned his back on the ship. For him rescue has stopped mattering.

spots.title: A famous model
spots.text: The man lying face down, one arm stretched over the planks, was posed by a young painter friend: Eugène Delacroix, who would later lead French Romantic painting.

spots.title: By the mast
spots.text: A man points toward the horizon and turns back to tell the others. Tradition sees here the two survivors Géricault interviewed, Corréard and Savigny.

spots.title: The signal
spots.text: At the very top, hoisted on a barrel by his companions, a Black man waves a cloth at the ship. In 1819, giving the summit of a history painting to an African sailor was a statement.

lesson.text: That last choice was deliberate. France still held slaves in its colonies, and the Medusa had been sailing to take back Senegal, a hub of that trade. Géricault moved in circles that wanted slavery abolished. He placed the hope of everyone on the raft in the arm of the man his society ranked lowest.
The model for the signaling figure is thought to be Joseph, a professional model from Haiti who was well known in Paris studios and posed for several painters of the time.

At the Salon the reaction split along political lines. Opponents of the restored monarchy praised it. Royalists saw an attack, and a pile of corpses. The jury gave Géricault a gold medal, but the state did not buy the canvas. He rolled it up, deeply discouraged.
In 1820 the painting crossed the Channel and was shown in a London exhibition hall for an entrance fee. About 40,000 people paid to see it, and Géricault took a share of the ticket money.
Now that you know the story, the corners of the canvas speak too. Wander through it on your own.

spots.title: The wave
spots.text: A dark wall of water lifts at the left edge, higher than the horizon. It is where the wind is taking them.

spots.title: Left behind
spots.text: A corpse lies at the edge with ropes and wreckage. Géricault studied bodies at a nearby hospital to get this gray-green skin.

spots.title: Sliding off
spots.text: A body wrapped in white trails into the sea at the lower right. The raft's edge is cut by the frame, as if the planks continued under your feet.

spots.title: White cloth
spots.text: A second man shakes a pale cloth against the sky. With the red and white fabric above, these are the brightest notes in a picture of browns.

spots.title: Reaching arms
spots.text: Men who can no longer stand drag themselves up on their neighbors. Count the hands lifted toward the right.

spots.title: The sail
spots.text: A patched sheet rigged to a short mast. Its huge brown shape repeats the storm clouds and takes up almost a quarter of the canvas.

lesson.text: The darkness you see is partly an accident. For his deepest shadows Géricault used bitumen, a tar-like brown that never fully dries. It has blackened and wrinkled over two centuries and cannot be reversed. In 1859 the Louvre had a full-size copy painted, in case the original was lost.

Géricault died in 1824, at 32, after riding accidents and a long illness. The Louvre bought the Raft from his estate that same year. On his tomb in Paris, a bronze relief reproduces it: the painter is remembered lying under the picture the state had once declined to buy.

quiz.question: Which moment of the disaster did Géricault choose to paint?
options: The first distant sighting of a ship
The survivors stepping aboard the Argus
quiz.explanation: He picked the morning a sail appeared on the horizon, before anyone knew if it would come.

quiz.question: Which way is the wind pushing the raft?
quiz.explanation: The sail swells to the left, away from the Argus on the right.

quiz.question: Who posed for the figure lying face down in the foreground?
quiz.explanation: Géricault's young friend Delacroix modeled for that figure.

quiz.question: Why has the painting become so dark?
options: It was damaged in a fire
Géricault used bitumen, which blackens with time
quiz.explanation: Bitumen never fully dries and has darkened and wrinkled.

quiz.question: What happened at the Salon of 1819?
options: The picture won a medal but the state did not buy it
The picture was refused by the jury
The king bought it on opening day
quiz.explanation: Géricault received a gold medal, yet no state purchase followed.

quiz.question: About how many people were put on the raft?
quiz.explanation: About 147 boarded the raft and fifteen were alive thirteen days later.

facts.text: The rescue ship fills the right side of the painting.
facts.explanation: The Argus is a tiny speck on the horizon.

facts.text: Géricault had the raft's carpenter build him a scale model.
facts.explanation: He used the model in his studio to get the raft right.

facts.text: The painting shows the survivors as thin and starving, exactly as reports described them.
facts.explanation: He gave them the muscular bodies of ancient statues, which critics noticed.
